content: The prevalence of tuberculosis (TB) and its associated outcomes, such as incidence and mortality, have not been fully established. However, a survey conducted in 2011, following World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, assessed a nationally representative sample of untreated TB cases. A total of 78 study sites were selected across the country using a probability proportional to size approach. All consecutive new pulmonary TB cases presenting at 39 selected health centers were enrolled in the study. Culture and drug sensitivity results were available for 1,050 out of the 1,080 enrolled patients, meeting the second benchmark for data completeness. In settings with low-level HIV epidemics, where routine HIV testing for most TB cases is not feasible, data collection through periodic surveys of TB cases is suggested. When routine surveillance systems are used to assess HIV testing coverage, it is essential that at least 80% of all notified TB cases have documented HIV status. Routine HIV testing and counseling provide significant benefits, including improved access to testing, early case detection, and timely treatment initiation for individuals living with HIV. In countries with separate TB and HIV surveillance systems, where confidentiality or other factors prevent routine documentation of HIV status in TB records, record linkage between the two systems should be performed to evaluate whether benchmarks are met. In low-level HIV epidemic settings, periodic or sentinel surveys every 2–3 years are recommended to collect data on HIV status among TB cases, following WHO policies on collaborative TB/HIV activities. Kenya, a country with a generalized HIV epidemic, has successfully recorded the HIV status of over 80% of TB patients since 2008. In 2011, 103,981 TB cases were reported, with 93% having documented HIV status. This achievement was facilitated by scaling up collaborative TB/HIV activities, including integrating HIV testing and antiretroviral therapy (ART) into TB facilities. Similarly, South Africa reported 389,974 TB cases in 2011, with 83% having documented HIV status, meeting the first benchmark for HIV surveillance among TB patients. The diagnosis of TB in children remains a significant challenge due to difficulties in obtaining sputum specimens and the reliance on clinical criteria and diagnostic tests. In high TB burden settings, most childhood TB cases occur in young children with paucibacillary disease, which is less likely to be detected through traditional sputum smear tests. Consequently, many childhood TB cases are underdiagnosed and underreported, leading to an underestimation of the true burden of TB in children. To address these challenges, national TB programs (NTPs) should assess the level of underreporting of childhood TB cases through inventory studies conducted within the past 10 years. If no recent studies have been conducted, planning for a new survey is recommended. Corrective actions, such as training and strengthening monitoring and evaluation systems, may be required to address gaps in reporting. Additionally, strategies to improve the diagnosis and reporting of childhood TB cases should be documented in national TB guidelines. In summary, achieving high coverage of HIV testing among TB patients and addressing the underreporting of childhood TB cases are critical for effective TB control. Collaborative efforts between TB and HIV programs, periodic surveys, and improved diagnostic and reporting systems are essential to meet global standards and benchmarks for TB surveillance.
